Lots of puzzles, and the rating still won't move? Puzzles help most when you do them in a way that carries over to real games.

Solve the whole line in your head before you click. Mix in slow, untimed puzzles, not only races. Redo the ones you miss a few days later until the idea is instant. In your own games, ask after every move: is there a check, a capture or a threat? And play some longer games, so you have time to spot the patterns you've learned.

slides.title: Lots of puzzles,
slides.sub: FIVE WAYS TO MAKE THEM COUNT

slides.title: Solve it before you click
slides.body: Find the whole line in your head first: your move, their best reply, your next move. Then play it. Guessing and clicking only trains guessing.
slides.note: If you can't say the line out loud, keep looking.

slides.title: Go slow, not fast
slides.body: Puzzle races are fun, but quick guesses don't build the careful looking you need in a real game. Mix in untimed puzzles and take your time.

slides.title: Redo the ones you miss
slides.body: A puzzle you got wrong is the most useful one. Note it, and try it again a few days later, until you see the idea at once.
slides.note: A pattern you see often becomes a habit.

slides.title: Look for it in your games
slides.body: In a puzzle you know there is a trick. In a game, nobody tells you. After each move, ask: is there a check, a capture or a threat?
slides.note: That one question turns puzzles into wins.

slides.title: Play longer games too
slides.body: Puzzles show you the ideas. Slower games give you time to spot them. Try a few 15 or 30-minute games each week.
slides.note: Then look back at your losses: which pattern did you miss?
